In The Iliad, Jove directs the Trojan War from Ida, favors and aids the Trojans, accepts necessary deaths, protects Hector, and answers Priam by arranging Hector’s return. In The Iliad, Jove rules Olympus, favors the Trojans for Thetis’s sake, directs the war, weighs fates, and ultimately arranges Hector’s burial. In Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Olympian Zeus becomes king of the gods, distributes divine offices, swallows Metis, gives birth to Athene, and fathers many descendants. In Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Zeus establishes his rule over gods and men, governs nature and justice, and shapes divine genealogies and human fate. In The Odyssey, Jove governs divine and mortal events, arranges Ulysses’s return, destroys his crew for sacrilege, answers prayers, and helps restore peace in Ithaca. In The Extant Odes of Pindar, Zeus is the Olympian king whose thunder, worship, and favor govern victory, prosperity, fame, cities, and human fortune. In Four Plays of Aeschylus, Zeus is both a harsh newly enthroned tyrant who binds Prometheus and the supreme protector, judge, and ancestor invoked by suppliants. In The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies, Zeus is the highest god who governs justice, vengeance, hospitality, prophecy, Orestes’ mission, and the restoration of order.

and 28 more works

In The Seven Plays in English Verse: Zeus is a god, high god, all-ruler, and King of the gods. He is father of Athena and Heracles, decrees the voyage to Troy, and values piety toward the gods above other qualities. In The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I: Jove, a god called the Sire, is protected by Corybantes as an infant and later dispenses fates in heaven. In Hecuba and other plays, Jove is the supreme ruler who grants victories and judgments, protects Hercules’s family, destroys Troy, and is questioned for failing to save Hercules and his children. In Hippolytus; The Bacchae: Zeus, Semelê’s divine partner and Dionysus’s father, saves the unborn Dionysus from the fire that kills Semelê, devises a secret birth, and protects the child from Hera with a likeness made from a fragment of the world-encircling fire. In The Argonautica, Zeus rules gods and mortals, determines fated events, protects strangers and suppliants, punishes violations, grants requests, and orders cleansing after Apsyrtus’s murder. In The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian: Jupiter Ammon, associated with a sacred grove, temple, oracle, cities, and Ammoni, promises Alexander the empire of the whole world. In The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Jupiter is the life-giving universal parent and ruling god who establishes order, conquers rebels, teaches sacred matters, and punishes impiety. In The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books: Ammon, a king in Libya, married Rhea and fathered Bacchus by Amalthaea, sending the child to Nysa for safety. In The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books: Jupiter Triphylius is presented as Saturn’s son, a king and conqueror who succeeded and defeated Saturn, ruled the world, punished the impious, benefited mankind, and treated subjects justly and courteously; they therefore called him Father. In The Aeneid, Jupiter enforces Aeneas’s destined journey to Italy, governs the gods and war, and compels the final peace between Trojans and Latins. In The Amores, or Amours: Jove is a ruler of the starry citadel and heavens, armed with lightnings and associated with transformations into bird, gold, and bull. In The Library, Zeus rules the sky, directs gods and mortals, punishes offenders, takes disguises, and fathers numerous gods, heroes, and rulers. In The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, Jupiter is the supreme god and ruler who judges, punishes, transforms, pursues, fathers, and intervenes in divine and mortal affairs. In The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, Jupiter judges, rewards, punishes, transforms, pursues, and deifies figures while advancing divine and heroic genealogies. In The Library, Zeus becomes sovereign of the sky, punishes enemies and impious people, directs transformations and events, and fathers many divine and heroic figures. In The Library: Belus, son of Libya and Poseidon and twin brother of Agenor, remained in Egypt, reigned over the Egyptians, married Anchinoe, daughter of Nile, and fathered the twins Egyptus and Danaus. In Description of Greece: Olympian Zeus is a deity worshipped at Olympia. Games honor him, and Elis built his temple and statue from spoils after destroying Pisa. In Description of Greece: is_created_by Polycletus [in white stone] The Argives erected a statue to Milichian Zeus after the people killed Bryas and the thousand picked men who supported him. In Description of Greece, Zeus is the central object of widespread civic and religious worship, associated with temples, images, rain, prophecy, oaths, guardianship, and fate. In Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II: Ammon is represented in square Hermæ with ram’s horns and by a statue; he has a temple near Epaminondas’ statue, where offerings, an altar, and an inscribed hymn honour him. In Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II: Friendly Zeus has a temple inside the precincts; his Polycletus-made statue resembles Dionysus, wearing buskins and holding a cup and thyrsus topped by an eagle. In Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Zeus is worshiped under many titles through temples, statues, rites, and local traditions, while also acting in myths involving Callisto, Demeter, and Hera. In Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II: Zeus Soter is represented in Pentelican-marble statuary seated on a throne beside Megalopolis; he ordered an annually chosen lad given to a dragon in Thespia and is called Saviour after its destruction. In Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II: Zeus Homagyrius is Zeus surnamed the Gatherer, with temple and statues at Ægium; the name recalls Agamemnon gathering famous men there to deliberate attacking Priam's realm. In The Fall of Troy, Zeus rules gods and men, directs fate and the Trojan war, restrains divine conflict, aids and opposes combatants, and destroys the Achaean walls. In Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Jupiter rules heaven and gods, judges mortal affairs, punishes corruption, protects favored people, and fathers or pursues heroes and women. In Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable: is_a chief deity of Thebes [king of the gods; the concealed sun] Amen Ra was a human-form deity crowned with a flat-topped cap and two long plumes, and he was generally described as King of the Gods and chief deity of Thebes. In Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone: Zeus is an all-seeing god and lord of heaven, invoked as witness and protector.

Jove in The Iliad

Homer · 749 to 724 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove is the supreme divine ruler: father and sire of gods and men, king of the gods and of Dodona, son of Saturn, lord of counsel, and husband and brother of Juno. From Ida, holding his thunderbolt, he watches and directs the war through Iris, Mercury, Apollo, portents, strength, and divine intervention. He initially favors the Trojans, orders Hector to wait for Agamemnon’s wounding, and promises him power to drive the Achaeans to their ships. Juno seduces him and causes him to sleep, briefly allowing Neptune to help the Achaeans. Jove grants Achilles that Patroclus will repel the battle from the ships but denies Patroclus a safe return. He pities his son Sarpedon yet accepts his death, honors him with bloody rain, shapes the fighting, and has Apollo prepare his body for transport. He gives Achilles’ helmet to Hector, protects Hector’s body, and ultimately hears Priam’s prayer, sends a favorable eagle and Mercury’s escort, and has Hector’s body returned. He also governs fortune and suffering through two urns.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

6 sections; each heading opens the text

BOOK XI.

Jove sends Discord to encourage the Achaeans and later watches the fighting from Mount Ida. He instructs Iris to tell Hector to wait until Agamemnon is wounded, promising Hector strength to kill the Achaeans until he reaches their ships and night falls.

BOOK XIV.

Jupiter is on the topmost crests of Mount Ida while the battle goes against the Achaeans. Juno arouses his passion, persuades him to lie with her, and causes him to fall asleep, leaving Neptune free to aid the Achaeans for a time.

BOOK XVI.

Jove hears Achilles’s prayer and grants that Patroclus will drive the battle away from the ships. He does not grant that Patroclus will return safely from the fight.

Now when Sarpedon saw his comrades, men who wore ungirdled

Jove pities Sarpedon and considers rescuing him, but accepts that Sarpedon must die. He sheds a rain of blood in honour of his son, influences the battle so that Patroclus drives back Hector and the Trojans, and orders Apollo to prepare Sarpedon’s body for transport to Lycia.

Meanwhile Patroclus, with many a shout to his horses and to

Zeus is said to place a high spirit in Patroclus and to govern counsels that humans cannot understand. He delivers Achilles’ helmet to Hector to wear.

So did he pray, and Jove the lord of counsel heard his prayer.

Jove hears Priam's prayer and sends an eagle as a favorable portent. He pities Priam and commands Mercury to escort him safely to Achilles, and Achilles says that Jove has also sent a message through his mother to have Hector's body returned.

Jove in The Iliad

Homer · 749 to 724 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove is a god: the supreme, most glorious ruler and king of gods and men, lord of counsel, lightning, thunder, storm-cloud, and heaven. A son of Saturn, he rules Olympus and Mount Ida, sits or watches from Olympus and Ida, possesses the aegis, thunderbolt, and golden scales that weigh fates, and is stronger and older than Neptune. He is husband of Juno and is named father of Apollo, Minerva, Mars, Hercules, Vulcan, Xanthus, Achilles through descent, Hector, and even Saturn. He is invoked as witness and guardian of covenants, prayers, sacrifices, and oaths, yet grants or withholds requests according to his own will. The central course of his action is his promise to Thetis: he will favor the Trojans until the Achaeans honor Achilles. He confirms this promise by bowing his head, then sends a lying dream to Agamemnon, accepts sacrifice without granting Agamemnon’s request, and helps bring about continued fighting. Although he considers peace and is invoked over the covenant, he orders Minerva to cause the Trojans to break their oaths. From Ida, he forbids divine intervention, weighs the battle toward the Trojans, sends thunder, lightning, wind, and portents, strengthens Hector, and drives the Achaeans back. He restrains Juno, Minerva, and Neptune while commanding Iris and Apollo to restore Hector and renew the Trojan attack. His favor is not simple or permanent. He protects Ilius and supports Hector to glorify Achilles, while foreseeing Hector’s death and refusing to destroy the Achaeans completely. He grants Achilles’s prayer that the Achaeans suffer, later pities Achilles, his horses, and Priam, and at times aids the Achaeans by clearing darkness or sending Minerva. Near the end he permits the gods to aid either side, weighs Hector’s doom against Achilles’s, and lets Hector’s doom sink. Finally, he orders that Hector’s body be released, instructs Thetis and Priam through Iris, and promises Priam safe passage to Achilles’s tent.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

30 sections; each heading opens the text

BOOK I.

Jove’s counsels are said to be fulfilled through the deaths caused by the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles. Calchas says that dreams come from Jove, and Agamemnon claims that Jove, the lord of counsel, will support him. Nestor says that Agamemnon’s greater authority comes from having more people under him by Jove’s favor.

to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,

Jove promises Thetis that he will bring about victory for the Trojans until the Achaeans honour Achilles. His promise troubles him because he expects Juno to quarrel with him, but he confirms it by bowing his head.

BOOK II.

Jove, thinking how to honor Achilles, sends a lying dream to Agamemnon and promises through it that the Achaeans will take Troy. He later remains the source of the prophecy that the Achaeans will succeed, though the dream conceals his plan for further fighting.

Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the

Jove accepts Agamemnon’s sacrifice but does not grant his prayer. Instead, he continues to increase the Achaeans’ toil.

BOOK III.

Jove is invoked as witness and guardian of the covenant, and the Trojans and Achaeans pray that oath-breakers and their children be punished. Menelaus and both armies also pray to Jove for victory over the one who began the war, but Jove does not yet grant their prayer.

BOOK IV.

Jove counsels with the gods on Olympus and suggests either renewing the fighting or making peace between the Trojans and Achaeans. He becomes angry with Juno but ultimately orders Minerva to make the Trojans break their oaths and attack the Achaeans.

The goddess went dazed and discomfited away, and Iris, fleet as

Jove is told that Diomed would now fight even with him. He smiles at Minerva's mockery of Venus and tells Venus to leave warfare to Mars and Minerva.

Now when the goddess Juno saw the Argives thus falling, she said

Jove approves Juno's plan to attack Mars and tells her to set Minerva against him. When Mars complains after being wounded, Jove rebukes him but orders Paeeon to heal him.

BOOK VII.

Jove is invoked as witness to the proposed terms of single combat and to the prayers of both armies. Agamemnon later calls Jove witness to the agreement allowing the dead to be burned.

Now in the twilight when it was not yet dawn, chosen bands of the

Jove is displeased by Neptune's remarks and answers that Neptune can destroy the Achaean wall after the Achaeans have gone home with their ships. He says the wall can be utterly effaced by casting it into the sea and covering the beach with sand.

Thus did they converse, and by sunset the work of the Achaeans

Jove boded ill for the Achaeans, the Trojans, and their allies by roaring with portentous thunder. His thunder caused pale fear, leading them to pour wine onto the ground and make offerings to the most mighty son of Saturn.

BOOK VIII.

Jove forbids the gods from interfering in the battle and threatens to punish anyone who helps the Trojans or Danaans. From Ida he tips his golden scales in favor of the Trojans, sends thunder and lightning against the Achaeans, answers Agamemnon’s prayer with an eagle portent, and repeatedly strengthens the Trojans.

Juno when she saw them had pity upon them, and at once said to

Jove sees Juno and Minerva setting out and sends Iris to order them back, threatening to lame their horses, destroy their chariot, and strike them with lightning. At Olympus, he asserts that all the gods together cannot overcome his power and says that Hector will continue fighting until he rouses Achilles at the ships over Patroclus’s body. He permits Juno and Minerva to advise the Argives but insists that the Argives will suffer heavily.

BOOK IX.

Jove is said to have promised Agamemnon that Troy would fall, but Agamemnon believes that this promise has been withdrawn. Jove is also said to have destroyed many Achaeans and to have shown favor to Achilles, while his lightning on the Trojan right encourages Hector.

When Hector saw Agamemnon quit the field, he shouted to the

Jove grants Hector a great triumph and causes the Trojans to gain the advantage at several points. He later ordains that neither side should have the advantage, and strikes fear into Ajax son of Telamon so that Ajax retreats.

BOOK XII.

Jove sends a mighty wind from Mount Ida that drives dust toward the ships, lulls the Achaeans into security, and gives victory to Hector and the Trojans. He also intends to give glory to Hector and has earlier shown the Trojans signs that encourage their attack.

Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him

Jove saves his son from destruction so that he will not fall by the ships' sterns. He later gives greater glory to Hector.

BOOK XIII.

Jove leaves Hector and the Trojans to their toil and turns his attention away from Troy, believing that no immortal will help either side. He intends to give victory to the Trojans and Hector in order to honor Achilles, but he does not intend to destroy the Achaean army completely.

Thus then did they fight as it were a flaming fire. But Hector

Jove is invoked in the exchanges between Ajax and Hector. He urges the Trojans onward to fight, and Ajax's challenge predicts that Hector will one day pray to Jove and the gods while fleeing.

BOOK XV.

Jove awakens on Ida and sees Hector wounded and the Trojans in confusion while Neptune leads the Achaeans. He orders Iris to make Neptune withdraw and Apollo to restore Hector and drive the Achaeans back, intending that Hector will eventually kill Patroclus and that Achilles will later kill Hector. He answers Nestor’s prayer with thunder as the Trojans renew their attack.

Now Patroclus, so long as the Achaeans and Trojans were fighting

Jove supports Hector and the Trojans, breaking Teucer’s bowstring and encouraging the Trojan attack. He intends to give Hector glory and allow him to set a ship on fire before later turning events in favor of the Achaeans.

BOOK XVII.

Jove’s will is described as stronger than that of mortals, and he gives victory or retreat as he chooses. He hides the brightness of the Achaeans’ helmets in a cloud while favoring the defense of Patroclus’s body, and he grants Hector temporary might while foreseeing Hector’s death.

Such fearful turmoil of men and horses did Jove on that day

Jove causes turmoil around Patroclus's body and initially gives the Trojans strength to continue killing the Achaeans. He pities Achilles' immortal horses, strengthens them so they can carry Automedon safely, and later sends Minerva to encourage the Danaans. At the two Ajaxes' request, he removes the darkness covering the battlefield.

BOOK XVIII.

Jove has granted Achilles’s earlier prayer that the Achaeans would suffer while Achilles stayed away from battle. He does not know that Iris has gone to Achilles at Juno’s command, and he later accuses Juno of having achieved her aim by rousing Achilles.

Now when Dawn in robe of saffron was hasting from the streams of

Jove is invoked in Agamemnon's oath and is said to have allowed Folly to blind men. He pities Achilles and the mourners, then sends Minerva to place nectar and ambrosia in Achilles so that hunger will not weaken him.

BOOK XX.

Jove summons the gods to council and tells them to support whichever side they favor. He remains on Olympus to watch the battle and warns that Achilles may overwhelm Troy if left unchecked. He is said to have loved the race of Dardanus, while he now hates the blood of Priam.

BOOK XXI.

Jove is named as the father of Xanthus and as the father of Achilles's ancestor Aeacus through his son Peleus's line. He has charged Apollo to support the Trojans until twilight and gives Neptune and Minerva permission to assist Achilles. Achilles also appeals to Jove when Xanthus threatens to drown him.

Xanthus was now beaten, so these two left off fighting, for Juno

Jove hears the gods fighting from Olympus and laughs with joy. He is described as the father of Minerva and Diana and as the husband of Juno, and he questions Diana after she returns weeping.

BOOK XXII.

Zeus watches Hector's pursuit and considers saving him, but agrees to Minerva's plan. He weighs the dooms of Achilles and Hector, and Hector's doom sinks toward Hades.

BOOK XXIV.

Jove decides that Hector’s body should be released and orders Thetis to tell Achilles to accept a ransom. He also sends Iris to Priam and promises that Mercury will escort Priam safely to Achilles’s tent.

Olympian Zeus in Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica

Hesiod · about 699 BC · the work’s page · read it where Olympian Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Olympian Zeus is king of the gods, urged by the blessed gods at Earth’s prompting to reign and distribute their dignities. He marries Metis, Themis, Eurynome, and lastly Hera; mates with Demeter and Leto; and loves Mnemosyne. After swallowing Metis to prevent her destined son taking royal power, he gives birth to Athene and fathers numerous gods, heroes, and children.

(ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and

Olympian Zeus was urged by the blessed gods, at Earth’s prompting, to reign over them and distribute their dignities. He married several goddesses, swallowed Metis to prevent her destined son from taking royal power, and gave birth to Athene from his own head. He also fathered numerous gods, heroes, and other children, including Apollo, Artemis, Hermes, Dionysus, and Heracles.

Zeus in Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica

Hesiod · about 699 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god, son of Cronos, father of gods and men, and supreme ruler of Olympus, the universe, mortals, and the deathless gods. Saved by Rhea from Cronos, he is concealed in Crete, grows up, frees those held by Cronos, overcomes Cronos, receives the thunderbolt, defeats the Titans and Typhoeus, distributes portions and privileges among the immortals, and establishes his reign. Thunder, lightning, the aegis, all-seeing wisdom, and the power to fulfil his will mark his authority. His rule governs human life as well as divine order: he gives or removes strength, wealth, prosperity, and right; sends rain, storms, snow, poverty, and fate; watches justice and punishes violence and crooked judgment. He hides life’s means and fire, creates Pandora as a punishment and plague for men, and can destroy corrupt people. He also responds to crises, arranging Persephone’s return in seasonal division when Demeter’s famine threatens mankind. Zeus’s family and unions shape much of the record. He is Hera’s husband and father of many figures, including Apollo, Athena, Hermes, Dionysus, Persephone, the Muses, Heracles, Aphrodite, Castor, Polydeuces, and others. He seduces or lies with Callisto, Io, Alcmena, Maia, Leda, and Europa; his actions produce children, transformations, gifts, and conflicts. He judges Hermes and Apollo, grants Teiresias prophetic power, honours Hecate without taking her former portion, and appoints divine offices. In later actions he plans the Trojan war with Themis, grants alternating immortality to Castor and Polydeuces, and intervenes in the battle of Frogs and Mice with thunder and crabs. Throughout, he is reverenced by the blessed as chiefest, greatest, mighty, loud-thundering lord of all.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

37 sections; each heading opens the text

The Hesiodic Poems

Zeus is saved by Rhea from being swallowed by Cronos, grows up, and overcomes Cronos. With the children released from Cronos, Zeus divides the universe among them and remains reigning after the war with the Titans and the overthrow of Typhoeus.

HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS

Zeus gives or takes away strength, fame, and prosperity, and he straightens or destroys as he wills. He hides the means of life and fire, creates Pandora as a punishment for men, watches justice, and punishes violence and crooked judgement.

Zeus sends autumn rains and may give a good result to ploughing and crops. Zeus of the Earth is invoked, together with Demeter, to make the grain sound and heavy, and his will is said to vary at different times.

(ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;

Zeus sends poverty upon men and governs the days that are to be observed for work. The speaker says that the outcomes of good and evil at sea rest with Zeus and Poseidon, and that Zeus sends autumn rain and storms.

THE ASTRONOMY

Zeus seduced Callisto and fathered Arcas. He delivered Callisto from being killed by her son and the Arcadians, then placed her among the stars as the Great Bear; he also placed Orion among the stars after Artemis and Leto prayed for him.

THE THEOGONY

Zeus is praised as the aegis-holder, father of gods and men, and supreme in power. After overcoming Cronos, he ruled in heaven, distributed portions and privileges among the immortals, and promised offices and rights to gods who fought against the Titans.

(ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.

Zeus honours Hecate above all and gives her splendid gifts. He does not take away any part of her original portion among the former Titan gods, and he makes her a nurse of the young.

(ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid

Zeus is concealed in Crete, grows quickly, and causes Cronos to restore his swallowed children. He frees the brothers of his father, receives the thunderbolt, leads the gods against the Titans, and rules over mortals and immortals.

(ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge

Zeus perceives the danger posed by Typhoeus and attacks him with thunder, lightning, and a lurid thunderbolt. He burns Typhoeus's heads, defeats him, and casts him into wide Tartarus.

THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701

Zeus fathers Graecus with Pandora, Magnes and Macedon with Thyia, and gives Endymion a special gift concerning the keeping of death. He carries Europa to Crete, fathers Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon by her, and is invoked in accounts of Bellerophon, the Harpies, Aeacus, and the fate of Thetis.

Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)

Zeus is presented as the father of Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen.

Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that

Zeus planned to mingle storm and tempest over the earth and destroy the race of mortal men, including the demigods, so that gods and mortals would no longer mate. He also laid toil and sorrow upon those born of immortals and mortals, directed the destructive storm, and struck Eetion with a thunderbolt.

THE SHIELD OF HERACLES

Zeus plans to beget a defender of gods and mortals and shares Alcmena’s bed during the same night that Amphitryon does. Through Zeus’s union with Alcmena, Heracles is born, and Zeus later gives Heracles power to slay Cycnus.

THE MELAMPODIA

Zeus selected Teiresias, together with Hera, to decide whether men or women receive greater pleasure in intercourse. After Hera blinded Teiresias for his answer, Zeus granted him the power of prophecy.

AEGIMIUS

Zeus seduced Io and, after being discovered by Hera, touched her and changed her into a white cow while swearing that he had not had intercourse with her. He was also said to have called Abantis Euboea after the cow.

THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501

Zeus, the thunder-lover and Father of men and gods, secretly gave birth to Dionysus far from men. He spoke, nodded with his dark brows, and ordained that mortals would sacrifice to Dionysus at his feasts.

II. TO DEMETER

Zeus gives Persephone to Hades and permits Hades to carry her away. He is described as the cloud-gathering, loud-thunderer Son of Cronos, and Demeter becomes angry with him for the abduction.

(ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back

Zeus recognizes that Demeter’s famine threatens mankind and the honors of the gods. He sends Iris, the gods, and finally Hermes to persuade or arrange for Persephone’s return, and he establishes the division of Persephone’s time between the underworld and the upper world.

III. TO DELIAN APOLLO

Zeus is Apollo’s father and receives him in his house, where he gives him nectar in a golden cup. Apollo declares that he will reveal Zeus’s unfailing will to men.

TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—

Zeus is Apollo’s father and the cloud-gathering ruler whose will sends a strong west wind to carry the Cretan ship toward Crisa. Hera also compares the strength of her desired child with Zeus’s strength.

IV. TO HERMES

Zeus secretly lies with Maia in her cave while Hera sleeps, and Hermes is born from their union. Hermes invokes Zeus as his father while defending himself against Apollo. Zeus is the judge before whom Hermes and Apollo are brought.

(ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the

Zeus hears Apollo’s accusation and Hermes’ denial, laughs at Hermes’ cunning, and orders them to search for the cattle together. He is pleased when they reconcile, confirms Apollo’s promises, and commands that Hermes receive authority over omens, animals, and service as messenger to Hades.

V. TO APHRODITE

Zeus is the greatest of the gods and holds the highest majesty, yet Aphrodite can lead his heart astray and mate him with mortal women. He causes Aphrodite to desire Anchises so that she will not mock the gods for mating with mortals. He gives Hestia honor instead of marriage, grants Tros horses in recompense for Ganymedes, makes Tithonus deathless without removing old age, and threatens to strike Anchises with a thunderbolt if he boasts of Aphrodite.

XII. TO HERA

Zeus is loud-thundering and delights in thunder. He is Hera’s brother and husband, and the blessed throughout high Olympus reverence and honour him.

XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED

Zeus is Heracles's father. He lay with Alcmena before Heracles was born.

XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI

Zeus is called Olympian Zeus and the dark-clouded Son of Cronos. He is said to have privately bent Leda to his will, and Castor and Polydeuces sprang from him.

XVIII. TO HERMES

Zeus, the Son of Cronos, lay with Maia at dead of night in her shadowy cave while Hera slept. Neither deathless god nor mortal man knew of this union.

XXIII. TO THE SON OF CRONOS, MOST HIGH

Zeus is praised as the chiefest and greatest of the gods, all-seeing, lord of all, and the fulfiller. He whispers words of wisdom to Themis as she leans toward him. The speaker asks Zeus to be gracious.

XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO

Zeus is named at the beginning and is called the source of kings. The Muses and Apollo are called children of Zeus.

XXVIII. TO ATHENA

Zeus bears Pallas Athene from his awful head while she is arrayed in warlike arms. He holds the aegis and is glad after Athene removes her heavenly armour.

XXXII. TO SELENE

Zeus is identified as the father of the Muses.

XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI

Zeus is described as the dark-clouded Son of Cronos and as the father of Castor and Polydeuces with Leda.

HOMER’S EPIGRAMS2601

Zeus is described as the father of the Hermus and as the giver of fate, including the speaker’s unhappy lot from birth. He is said to hold the aegis, to have enabled the people of Phricon to build Aeolian Smyrna, and to send snow in winter. Zeus also rules on high as the god of strangers, whose vengeance follows those who sin against him, and he is called the lord of guests and the guest-table.

FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS

Zeus is introduced by Eumelus as dancing in the midst of others, where he is called the Father of men and gods.

THE CYPRIA

Zeus plans with Themis to bring about the Trojan war in order to relieve the earth of its burden of men. He sends Hermes to lead Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Alexandrus for judgment, and he gives Polydeuces immortality every other day after Castor’s death.

THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE

Zeus summons the gods to view the armies and asks who will aid the Frogs or the Mice. He watches the battle, becomes concerned when Slice-snatcher threatens to destroy the Frogs, frightens both armies with his thunderbolt, and finally sends the crabs to help the Frogs.

Jove in The Odyssey

Homer · about 632 to 599 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove is a god, son of Saturn, king and chief of the gods and men, ruler of heaven and earth, and lord of all. He is married to Juno and is father of Minerva and, as stated by Vulcan, Venus. As guardian of suppliants, strangers, beggars, foreigners in distress, and hospitality, he is invoked in prayers and as a witness. He governs events by divine will, sometimes bringing misfortune, panic, storms, shipwreck, and destruction by thunderbolt. At the gods’ meeting, he explains Neptune’s persecution of Ulysses and supports planning Ulysses’ return. Later he decrees that Ulysses return home without divine or human convoy, orders Mercury to command Calypso to release him, and declares that the Phaeacians will honor and transport him. He agrees to punish Ulysses’ crew for slaughtering the sun-god’s cattle, then raises a storm and destroys their ship, killing the men. He answers Ulysses’ request for a sign with thunder and hears the miller-woman’s prayer against the suitors. At the end, he supports peace: Ulysses is to continue ruling, opponents are to forgive the massacre, and a fiery thunderbolt reinforces Minerva’s command to end the war.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

6 sections; each heading opens the text

The Odyssey / BOOK I

Olympian Jove presides over the meeting of the gods and speaks first about Aegisthus. He explains that Neptune persecutes Ulysses because Ulysses blinded Polyphemus and agrees that the gods should plan Ulysses’ return.

BOOK V

Jove presides over the gods’ council and decrees that Ulysses must return home. He sends Mercury to order Calypso to release Ulysses and declares that the Phaeacians will honor and transport him.

“Here she ended, and dawn enthroned in gold began to show in heaven,

Jove agrees to punish Ulysses's crew for killing the sun-god's cattle. After the ship leaves the island, he raises a storm and destroys the ship with thunderbolts, killing the men.

Jove is said to have caused the terrible expedition to Troy and to have devised misfortune for the disguised Ulysses. He sends panic during the Egyptian defeat, destroys the Phoenician ship with thunderbolts, protects strangers, and is invoked as a witness and in prayers.

BOOK XX

Jove hears Ulysses's request for signs and answers with thunder from the clouds. He also hears the miller-woman's prayer that the suitors will never dine in Ulysses's house again.

Jove agrees with Minerva that Ulysses should continue to rule and that the opposing parties should forgive the massacre of their sons and brothers. He sends a fiery thunderbolt before Minerva to reinforce her command that the war must cease.

Zeus in The Extant Odes of Pindar

Pindar · 497 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is an Olympian, eternal god: son of Kronos and Rhea, husband of Hera, king of heaven and the immortals, lord of Olympus, Olympia, and the Olympic games. He dwells above clouds on the Kronian hill and is marked above all by thunder, white, red, and bickering lightning, through which he gives signs, confirms prophecies, stops expeditions, kills or buries opponents, and governs events. His authority extends over human fortune, excellence, fame, prosperity, laws, and the outcomes of things; he can humble pride, sustain those who honor him, and protect cities, lands, families, and victors. The records repeatedly present him as the god of athletic worship and victory. Sacred groves, altars, libations, ordinances, crowns, and songs at Olympia and Nemea belong to him. Petitioners ask him to preserve honor, grant prosperity and old age, protect Aigina, Corinth, Kamarina, Aitna, and other places, and make victories renowned. He is also associated with music and poetry and is invoked by bards. Zeus's family is extensive. He fathers Athene, Semele, Achilles, Lokros, Epaphos, Herakles, Aiakos, Polydeukes, and others; he is ancestor of the Aiakidai and connected with Aigina, Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles. He grants Polydeukes a choice involving Kastor, answers Herakles’ prayer, and promises Peleus a sea-bride. His actions include raining gold on Rhodes, giving Sicily to Persephone, causing and ending a flood, ordaining destinies, and defending or favoring communities. From his origins as Kronos’s son, the account unfolds through his cosmic rule, kinship, judgments, benefactions, and continuing worship as the powerful source of victory, order, and human fortune.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

30 sections; each heading opens the text

notes

Zeus was the deity to whom the Olympic games were sacred.

II.

Zeus is invoked as lord of Olympus, the chief games, and the ford of Alpheos. He is asked to protect the native fields of Theron's people for their future sons, and he is described as judging the guilty souls beneath the earth.

III.

The precinct of Zeus is the place to which Herakles brought the olive tree as a common shade and crown for valorous deeds. The games and their altars are associated with Zeus's worship.

IV.

Zeus is invoked as the hurler of unfaltering thunderbolts and the most high son of Kronos. He is asked to receive the band of triumph for the Olympian victory and to be gracious to the prayers associated with what shall come.

V.

Zeus is invoked as guardian of the city, seated above the clouds on the Kronian hill and associated with the Alpheos and Ida’s holy cave. The speaker prays that he will glorify Kamarina with the renown of brave men and grant Psaumis a serene old age.

VII.

Zeus is the father of Athene and is said to have rained golden snow upon Rhodes when Athene was born. He also caused a yellow cloud to rain gold on the Rhodians and is asked to glorify Diagoras and the Olympian victory hymn from Mount Atabyrios.

VIII.

Zeus is invoked as the wielder of white lightning, the guardian of Timosthenes’ and Alkimedon’s house, and the god who grants answers concerning human excellence. He is also credited with granting Olympic glory to the family and is asked to preserve its honor and protect it from disease.

IX.

Zeus is praised as the god of the red or bickering lightning-flash. He brought about the ebb of the flood and fathered the child born to the daughter of Opöeis, and by his decree Pyrrha and Deukalion established the city of Protogeneia.

XI.

Zeus gives the ordinances that inspire Pindar to sing of the Olympic games. Herakles dedicates the sacred grove to Zeus, and Zeus is celebrated as the loud-pealing god of thunder, lightning, and victory.

XIII.

Zeus is addressed as the sovereign of Olympia and as the father of Athene. He is asked to protect Corinth, preserve Xenophon’s favourable fortune, and grant honour and prosperity to the Oligaithidai.

I.

Zeus is invoked as the defender of Mount Etna and as the one with whom the outcomes of things rest. The speaker asks him to favor the mountain, grant good fortune to Aitna, and silence the Phoenician and Tuscan war-cry.

II.

Zeus is the husband of Hera and makes the cloud-phantom in her form to trap Ixion. He is also described as a god who brings down human pride and gives glory to others.

III.

Zeus is described as the father of Apollo and as one whose sons' wrath is not idle. He killed Asklepios and the man restored by him, striking them with lightning because Asklepios had brought a dead man back to life.

IV.

Zeus confirms the significance of the earth clod given to Euphemos with a peal of thunder. Jason also invokes Zeus before the Argonauts begin their voyage, and thunder and lightning answer as favorable signs.

VIII.

Zeus is named with Aiakos, Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles in the final prayer for the protection of Aigina and its city.

IX.

Zeus is associated with the chosen garden and broad meadow-lands of Libya where Apollo would establish Kyrene. Aristaios is described as being made like an immortal, a Zeus or a holy Apollo, through the care of the divine powers.

Nemean Ode I

Zeus is called Aitnaian and lord of Olympus. He gave the isle of Sicily to Persephone, and Zeus’s son is said to have foretold Herakles’ divine reward and dwelling among the immortals.

Nemean Ode II

Nemeaian Zeus is invoked as the deity whose grove witnessed Timodemos laying the foundation of his victory. The citizens are also told to celebrate him at the games of Zeus.

Nemean Ode III

Zeus is called the king of heaven, and the divine Muse is identified as his daughter. The blood of Aiakos’ race is also said to belong to Zeus, as do the games celebrated by the song.

Nemean Ode IV

Zeus the son of Kronos is invoked at the beginning of the hymn. He is also said to have ordained Peleus's destiny.

Nemean Ode V

Zeus is named as the ancestor of the Aiakidai and as the grandsire whose altar stood on Aigina. Zeus Hellenios received the prayers of the Aiakidai for Aigina's good men and fame in shipping; Zeus also promised Peleus a sea-bride from among the Nereids.

Nemean Ode VII

Zeus is invoked when Nemea is named and is celebrated as the king of the gods. He is said to have fathered Aiakos by a mortal mother and to have made him ruler of cities.

Nemean Ode IX

Zeus did not speed the expedition against Thebes, but warned the warriors through flashing lightning to halt their journey. He later buried Amphiaraos and his horses by splitting the deep-breasted earth with a thunderbolt, and the speaker asks Zeus to grant Aitna good laws and lasting prosperity.

Nemean Ode X

Zeus fathered Polydeukes and entered Alkmene's hall in the likeness of Amphitryon. He killed Idas with a thunderbolt and offered Polydeukes the choice between dwelling wholly in Olympos or sharing equal time with Kastor beneath the earth and in heaven.

Isthmian Ode III

Zeus is the source of all high excellence among mortals. Those who honor him may enjoy lasting happiness, while prosperity does not remain steadfast with perverse minds.

Isthmian Ode IV

Zeus is said to approve the might of men and to grant or order human outcomes. He is also called lord of all, and his grace gives poets material for praising great warriors.

Isthmian Ode V

The first libation was made to Zeus after victory at Nemea, and a third is planned for Zeus the Saviour and the Olympic god. Zeus answered Herakles’ prayer by sending a mighty eagle and granting Telamon a brave son.

Isthmian Ode VII

Zeus favored Aigina and Thebe, the two daughters of Asopos. Zeus fathered Aiakos with Aigina, and Zeus was one of the gods who desired Thetis as a bride before hearing the oracle concerning her son.

FRAGMENT OF A DITHYRAMB,

The singer (speaker) says that the singer (speaker) has come from the house of Zeus.

FRAGMENT OF A SONG WITH ACCOMPANIMENT OF DANCE

Zeus is invoked in a prayer concerning the meaning of the eclipse. The speaker asks for the event to bring good fortune to Thebes.

Zeus in Four Plays of Aeschylus

Aeschylus · 471 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god and supreme ruler of gods and men: son of Cronos, newly enthroned after overthrowing Cronos, governing from heaven with thunder, lightning, eagle, and authority over divine purpose and the Fates. In the records of Prometheus Bound, he is a harsh, suspicious tyrant whose self-sought rule is enforced through punishment. He condemns and binds Prometheus for aiding humanity, intends humanity's destruction early in his reign, and commands Hermes to force from Prometheus the secret of a marriage destined to bring Zeus down. Though powerful and ruthless, he cannot evade ordained fate; Prometheus foretells that Zeus's own counsels and a future marriage will produce a child who overcomes him, while also saying Zeus will someday need Prometheus and become milder. Elsewhere, Zeus is chiefly invoked as protector and arbiter: lord and guard of suppliants, strangers, kinship, guestright, purity, justice, and the balance of fate. The Danaids appeal to him for rescue from ravishment and hated marriage, trusting his will to accomplish its result and fearing his wrath against those who scorn divine claims. He punishes hubris and is called saviour and guardian of mortals' purity. He is also invoked through his bolt against enemies. His bond with Io links him to the Danaids: he loves and approaches her as a bull, her persecution and exile follow, and in Egypt he restores her by touch and fathers Epaphus. Through Io and Epaphus he becomes ancestor of the Danaids. Thus the records present both an all-powerful guardian sought by the distressed and a newly established ruler whose violence, tyranny, and threatened overthrow shape the conflict with Prometheus.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

INTRODUCTION

Zeus condemns Prometheus for his aid to humanity and enforces the punishment through Hephaestus and the agents Strength and Violence. His rule is threatened by a secret known to Prometheus, and the unit distinguishes the Zeus of Prometheus Bound from the more benevolent or different conceptions appearing elsewhere in Aeschylus.

THE SUPPLIANT MAIDENS / DEDICATION

Zeus loves Io and approaches her in the shape of a bull despite Argus’s watch. In Egypt, he restores Io to herself by touching her and fathers Epaphus.

The Suppliant Maidens

Zeus is invoked as lord and guard of suppliant hands, protector of mortals' purity, and savior of the distressed. The Chorus also recalls that Zeus fathered Epaphus through Io and trusts that his will will bring about its appointed result.

Enter the KING OF ARGOS.

Zeus loved Io, touched her at Canopus and Memphis, and fathered Epaphus with her. He is invoked as lord of kinship, the suppliants, and justice, and as the power whose will guides all counsels and deeds.

Re-enter DANAUS.

Zeus is invoked as lord of suppliants, guests, purity, the hospitable board, and the balance of fate. The Danaids ask him to protect them from the ravisher and from the hated marriage, while Danaus warns that those who scorn the gods will suffer for it.

Enter on one side THE SPY; on the other ETEOCLES and the SIX

Zeus is invoked as the power whose bolt may strike Capaneus and whose might stands against Typhon. His image appears on Hyperbius's shield, and the Chorus looks to his heavenly bolts to destroy the attacking foemen.

PROMETHEUS BOUND

Zeus rules the gods and men as a newly established, harsh, and suspicious ruler. He orders Prometheus’s binding and punishes him for aiding mortal men, but Prometheus says that Zeus will eventually need his help and learn a milder mood.

[_Exit OCEANUS._]

Zeus rules from a self-sought throne with a stern and ruthless power. Prometheus says that Zeus cannot avoid the fate ordained for him, though he refuses to reveal what that fate is.

Enter IO, horned like a cow.

Zeus desired Io, and his passion led to her persecution by Hera and her banishment from home. Prometheus foretells that Zeus will fall through his own counsels when a child born from a future marriage overcomes him.

[_Exit IO._]

Zeus commands Hermes to learn from Prometheus what marriage will cause his fall from supremacy. He is portrayed as refusing to soften at Prometheus’s words and as possessing the power to inflict further punishment, including the destruction of the rocky ravine with thunder and lightning.

Zeus in The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies

Aeschylus · 457 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is the highest, ruling god: father of the Olympian gods, Athena, Orestes, and Electra; lord of heaven, hospitality, fulfilment, justice, vengeance, and the ultimate cause and finisher of all. He brings wisdom through suffering, punishes sinners and violated hospitality, and is credited with Troy’s fall and the Greeks’ return. He wills Asclepius’s death as a warning. As protector of Orestes and Electra, he is invoked to restore their house and secure justice. Through Apollo’s prophetic office, Zeus commands Orestes to avenge his father, with his command outweighing oaths. Finally, as Athena’s champion and the authority behind Orestes’ trial, his power supports judgment, parley, and peace.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

5 sections; each heading opens the text

AGAMEMNON

Zeus is praised as the highest divine power who brings knowledge through affliction and strikes down the sinner. The Chorus credits him with the victory over Troy and invokes him as lord of heaven and hospitality.

_Enter_ HERALD

Zeus is invoked as the ruling god who helped bring the Greeks home and who judges wrongdoing. The Chorus says that Zeus avenges the wronged husband and does not tolerate violated hospitality.

ORESTES (_approaching suddenly_)

Zeus is invoked as the protector and father of Orestes and Electra, the orphaned children of Agamemnon. Orestes and Electra ask Zeus to restore their house and aid their cause.

[_Re-enter Athena, with twelve Athenian citizens_.

Zeus is presented by Apollo as the source of the oracle commanding Orestes to avenge his father. Apollo says that oaths do not prevail over Zeus’s command and that Zeus pities Orestes because of his father’s fate.

CHORUS

Zeus is presented as Athena’s champion and as the source of authority behind the judgment in the trial of Orestes. His will is said to have been shown through his prophet-god, and he is invoked as the king of parley whose power helps secure peace.

Zeus in The Seven Plays in English Verse

Sophocles · 449 to 429 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god, high god, all-ruler, and King of the gods. He is father of Athena and Heracles, decrees the voyage to Troy, and values piety toward the gods above other qualities. Characters invoke him as the supreme authority who sees mortal actions, secures his kingdom, witnesses oaths and prophecies, hears pleas for relief, and is called on to punish wrongdoing. Heracles speaks of Zeus's intentions, while Zeus's promises are linked to the benefit of Oedipus's burial to Athens.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

4 sections; each heading opens the text

CHORUS.

Zeus is invoked as a god who sees the ways of mortals and as the ruler whose kingdom and authority the Chorus asks to remain secure. Oedipus also calls on Zeus in distress when he realizes the possible identity of Laius's killer.

CHORUS.

Zeus is invoked as the supreme ruler and as Heracles's divine father. Heracles appeals to Zeus for relief from his torment and calls on him as witness when Hyllus swears to obey.

MONODY.

Zeus is invoked by Philoctetes in pleas and oaths. Heracles claims to speak with authority about what Zeus intends and says that Zeus values piety above all.

_Enter_ THESEUS.

Zeus is invoked as a witness to Oedipus's prophecy and as the divine power whose promises would make Oedipus's burial beneficial to Athens. Oedipus also invokes Zeus when praying that Creon be punished.

Jove in The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I

Euripides · 437 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove, a god called the Sire, is protected by Corybantes as an infant and later dispenses fates in heaven. He fathers Diana, Bacchus, and Epaphus; after lightning kills Semele, he receives infant Bacchus and conceals him in his thigh until birth. He is linked to Venus and Love, gives Helen away as the bride’s κύριος, allies with and rightly favors Chorus, and is invoked by Phædra as ancestor and destroyer.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

4 sections; each heading opens the text

CHORUS.

Jove was the marriage partner through whom Bacchus was produced, and Epaphus is called Jove's progeny.

CHORUS, PHÆDRA.

Jove is invoked in descriptions of Venus and Love, and Hippolytus questions why Jove allowed women to exist. Phædra calls Jove her ancestor and asks him to destroy the Nurse with fire.

THE BACCHÆ.

Jove is identified as the father of Bacchus and the source of the lightning that killed Semele. The Chorus says that Jove later received the infant Bacchus and concealed him in his thigh until his birth was completed.

CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant

Jupiter is called the speaker's ally, and the speaker trusts that Jupiter rightly favors the speaker. The speaker believes the gods will not appear inferior to men.

Jove in Hecuba and other plays

Euripides · about 429 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove is a god and supreme ruler of Heaven, described as ruling inferior gods, authoring success and divine judgments, and punishing base deeds and pride. He is father of Hercules, Hebe, and Helen, grandfather of Hermione, and father of Hercules’ children through Hercules. His altar, erected by Hercules, protects Hercules’ family, and he is invoked for their defense. He aids Athens against Argos and overthrows Troy. Yet Amphitryon and the Chorus question his justice and hatred when he does not save Hercules or his children. By the end, he is invoked as Zeus for victory and renewed strength.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

3 sections; each heading opens the text

HERCULES DISTRACTED.

Jove is presented as Hercules’ divine father and as the god whose altar protects the family. Amphitryon appeals to Jove to defend his son, then accuses him of being unjust or lacking wisdom because he has not saved Hercules’ children.

IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.

Jove is identified as Hercules’ father, and the Chorus calls him mighty Jove. The Chorus asks why Jove has hated his son and allowed him to be plunged into such troubles.

SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.

Zeus is invoked as the author of the victory and as a god whose judgments punish pride. Iolaus prays to Zeus for the temporary restoration of his youthful strength.

Zeus in The Argonautica

Apollonius Rhodius · 299 to 200 BC · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god, king of gods, ruler of the Olympians, and ruler and observer of mortal affairs. He determines events by divine fate or counsel, including Heracles’ labors for Eurystheus and Polyphemus’s founding of Cius. He acts as messenger-sender, father of Athena, god of strangers and suppliants, god of wrath who aids slayers of men, and Zeus the Cleanser. He punishes Phineus with blindness and lingering old age for revealing divine will too fully, while granting the sons of Boreas tireless strength to pursue the Harpies. He is invoked in libations, receives altars and sacrifices, gives Sinope a home and grants her request for virginity, and is credited with rescuing Phrixus and his sons. He sends the north wind, storm, and shipwreck against the sons of Phrixus, then ends the rain at sunrise. Finally, angered by Apsyrtus’s killing, he decrees cleansing through Circe’s counsels and many woes before the perpetrators’ return.

Jupiter in The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books

Diodorus Siculus · 59 to 29 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter is described as a spirit or quickening influence that gives life to living creatures, making him the common parent of all things; he is also an elemental god, a terrestrial god who ruled Egypt, and is called Belus, Ammon, and the Egyptian name for that life-giving influence. In the Cretan account, he is the son of Saturn and Rhea, hidden in Ida by Rhea and raised by Curetes and nymphs on milk, honey, and Amalthea's milk. After succeeding Saturn, receiving instruction from Olympus, and becoming king of Egypt, he became lord of the universe and ruled Olympus, the heavens, and storms. His rule is marked by justice, lawful courts, peace, good government, communities, and punishment of violent and impious people. He conquered the Titans and fought giants who rebelled against the gods. He is associated with many descendants: Dionysius by Semele, Minos and Rhadamanthus by Europa, and others by Io, Electra, Hamalia, Carme, and Scythes's mother. He revealed sacred mysteries to Jasion, initiated strangers, and privately instructed Minos. When Semele asked him to appear in thunder and lightning, she was consumed, and he arranged for their infant to be taken to Nysa. He also struck Phaeton with a thunderbolt.

8 sections; each heading opens the text

We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them

Jupiter is the Egyptian name for the spirit or quickening influence that gives life to living creatures and is therefore regarded as the common parent of all things. Jupiter is also listed among the terrestrial gods who once ruled Egypt and is called Ammon by some.

From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who

Jupiter is presented in the Greek account as the father of Osiris or Dionysius through Semele. He is also named as one of the gods against whom the giants rebelled and with whom Osiris was associated in Egyptian identifications.

The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^

Jupiter was the son of Saturn and Rhea and was later advanced to positions of honor by Dionysius. He became king after receiving instruction from Olympus, was made king of Egypt, and later became lord of the universe; the text also names him as the father of the second Bacchus by Io and of the third Bacchus by Semele.

DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.

Jupiter loved Semele and fathered Dionysius by her. When he appeared to her in thunder and lightning at her request, Semele was consumed by the flames, after which Jupiter arranged for the infant to be taken to Nysa.

CHAP. III.

Jupiter is named as the father of Saon in one account and as the father of Dardanus, Jasion, and Harmonia with Electra. He revealed the sacred mysteries to Jasion and is said to have initiated strangers into them.

Nireus, the son of Charops and Aglaia, was, in after times^

Jupiter was said to have conquered the Titans and to have fathered Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus by the nymph Hamalia. His sons were among those preserved by fleeing to higher ground during the inundation of Rhodes.

CHAP. IV.

Jupiter was hidden on Ida by Rhea and raised by the Curetes and nymphs on milk, honey, and the milk of the goat Amalthea. After succeeding Saturn, he promoted justice, lawful courts, peace, and good government, punished violent and impious persons, established communities, and was credited with ruling the heavens and storms; he also fought the giants.

Vulcan, they say, found out the working of iron, brass, silver, and

Jupiter was said to be the father of Europa's sons Minos and Rhadamanthus and of the elder Hercules. He was also named as the father of Britomartis through Carme and was said to have privately instructed Minos in a cave.

Jupiter Triphylius in The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books

Diodorus Siculus · 59 to 29 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter Triphylius first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter Triphylius is presented as Saturn’s son, a king and conqueror who succeeded and defeated Saturn, ruled the world, punished the impious, benefited mankind, and treated subjects justly and courteously; they therefore called him Father. After death he was placed in the highest heavens, worshipped as the chiefest god and supreme lord, and called Zeus or Zena for teaching men proper living. He fathers Hercules through Alcmena after taking Amphitryon’s shape and lengthening the night, declares the day’s child king of the Persians, arranges Hercules’s immortality through twelve labours, orders him to obey Eurystheus, and later calls him an Olympian god. He imprisons Prometheus, strikes Salmoneus and Asclepius, purifies Ixion, and fathers Aeacus by Aegina. His temple in Panchsea is greatly revered, and Panara’s citizens call themselves his suppliants.

Jupiter, the son of Saturn, was said to have treated his subjects justly and courteously and was therefore called Father. He succeeded Saturn, defeated him in battle with the aid of the Titans’ opposition, conquered the world, punished the impious, and benefited mankind. After his death he was placed in the highest heavens and worshipped as a god and supreme lord of the earth, receiving the name Zena from his instruction of men in proper living.

Jupiter fathers Hercules with Alcmena after deceiving her by taking the shape of Amphitryon, and he lengthens the night threefold. He declares that the child born that day will be king of the Persians, later arranges that Hercules may gain immortality through twelve labours, and commands him to obey Eurystheus.

The figure identified in this record as Jupiter struck Salmoneus and Asclepius with thunderbolts. He also purified Ixion after Ixion killed Hesioneus, and by Aegina fathered Aeacus.

CHAP. III.

Jupiter Triphylius is worshipped in Panchsea, where his temple is held in great veneration. The citizens of Panara call themselves his suppliants.

Jupiter in The Aeneid

Virgil · 28 to 18 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter is the supreme god, ruler of heaven and earth, king and father of gods and mortal men, divine protector and judge, and husband of Juno. Father of Venus and Sarpedon, he governs fate, commands other gods and messengers, and presides over the gods’ council. His central concern is the unalterable destiny of Aeneas: Aeneas must reach Italy, defeat its nations, establish cities, and begin the line leading through Ascanius, Alba Longa, and Romulus to Rome’s immortal empire. He comforts Venus, arranges a friendly reception in Carthage, and sends Mercury to make Aeneas leave Dido and pursue the promised Latian lands. He answers prayers and intervenes through signs and weather, extinguishing the Trojan fleet’s fire with storms, lightning, thunder, and rain, and favoring Ascanius with thunder. During the war, he orders Iris to remove Turnus, summons the gods, forbids divine factions, and declares Trojans and Rutulians equally subject to fortune. He allows temporary reprieves, including Turnus’s flight, but insists that fixed fate cannot be changed, as even Sarpedon cannot be saved from death. At the end, he compels Juno to stop aiding Turnus and establishes peace: Latins retain their name, customs, and language, Trojans merge with them, and Troy’s name disappears.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

8 sections; each heading opens the text

BOOK I

Jupiter comforts Venus and confirms that Aeneas will reach Italy, defeat its nations, and establish cities. He outlines the succession from Ascanius and Alba Longa to Romulus and Rome, and sends Mercury to secure a friendly reception for the Trojans in Carthage.

BOOK IV

Jupiter hears Hyarbas's prayer and sees Dido and Aeneas absorbed in their love at Carthage. He sends Mercury to order Aeneas to leave Libya and pursue the future empire and fame destined for Ascanius and the Romans.

The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;

Jove commands Aeneas to leave the Tyrian court and seek the promised Latian lands. His command keeps Aeneas from yielding to Dido’s pleas.

Thus far the sacred sports they celebrate:

Jove answers Aeneas’s prayer by sending southern storms, lightning, thunder, and heavy rain that extinguish the fleet’s fire. His will also directs Aeneas to separate the fearful from those destined to continue the voyage.

Now rose the ruddy morn from Tithon’s bed,

Jupiter hears Ascanius’s prayer and gives a favorable sign by bowing the heavens and thundering on the left. He later commands Iris to force Turnus out of the Trojan camp.

BOOK X

Jupiter summons the gods to council and rebukes them for prolonging the war after he had commanded peace. He forbids divine factions, declares that Trojans and Rutulians are equally subject to fortune, and leaves each side to its fate.

But, in another part, th’ Arcadian horse

Jupiter tells his queen that mortal life has fixed limits and recalls that even his son Sarpedon could not be saved from death. He permits Juno to remove Turnus from immediate danger but warns that she cannot change the fates or save him from destined death.

Now Turnus rolls aloof o’er empty plains,

Jove tells Juno that Aeneas's destiny cannot be resisted and orders her to cease aiding Turnus. He agrees that the Latins will retain their name, customs, and language, while the Trojans will merge with them and Troy's name will disappear.

Jove in The Amores, or Amours

Ovid · 15 BC · the work’s page · read it where Jove first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jove is a ruler of the starry citadel and heavens, armed with lightnings and associated with transformations into bird, gold, and bull. Fostered by Cretans and fed milk in infancy, he later would defend heaven against Giants; Naso leaves that theme for his shut-out mistress and seeks Jove’s pardon.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

2 sections; each heading opens the text

BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.

Jove would have hurled his lightnings in defense of the realms of heaven while Naso sang of the Giants. Naso abandoned Jove and his weapons when his mistress shut her door, and he asks Jove to pardon him.

ELEGY X.

Jove, who rules the starry citadel of the world, drank milk with tender lips as a little child in Crete.

Zeus in The Library

Apollodorus · AD 1 to 200 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god, son of Cronus and Rhea, born in a cave of Dicte in Crete, fed by nymphs and guarded by Curetes. After making war on the Titans and shutting them in Tartarus, he receives dominion over the sky by lot. He becomes Hera’s husband, though their relationship includes his fear of her and his binding and hanging her from Olympus. He possesses the aegis, ordains oaths by Styx, appoints gods and Hermes to duties, judges disputes, and repeatedly directs divine and mortal affairs. His rule is marked by conflict and punishment: he fights Typhon and giants, casts Etna on Typhon, and uses thunderbolts against Aesculapius, Idas, Iasion, Salmoneus, Capaneus, and others. He binds Ixion, orders Prometheus nailed to the Caucasus, causes a flood to destroy the men of the Bronze Age, transforms or punishes figures such as Io, Ceyx, Alcyone, and Lycaon, and strikes Ulysses’s ship after the slaughter of the Sun’s cattle. He also aids or orders Hermes in many missions, appoints Aeolus keeper of the winds, and determines outcomes involving Adonis, Atreus, Alexander, and Attica. Zeus has numerous unions, often through disguises or abduction, and fathers many gods, heroes, and rulers. His children include Hermes, the Muses, Helen, Pollux, Castor, Aeacus, Iasion, Dardanus, Dionysus, Perseus, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, Amphion, Zethus, Pan, Hellen, and Lacedaemon. He carries Europa to Crete as a bull, approaches Leda and Nemesis as a swan, impregnates Danae as a stream of gold, and takes Aegina away. The records conclude by emphasizing his broad intervention in the affairs of gods, heroes, cities, births, punishments, and major events.

Zeus ordered Hermes to take Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Alexander for judgment. Some accounts say that Alexander abducted Helen in accordance with Zeus’s will so that his daughter would become famous, while another account says Zeus sent a phantom of Helen to Troy.

IIJ.—Myrus oF THE ORIGIN OF FIRE

Zeus is identified by Hesiod and Hyginus as the source from whom Prometheus stole the fire given to men. His citadel is said to be guarded by dreadful warders, preventing Prometheus from entering it directly in Plato’s account.

Erysichthon, son of Cecrops by

Zeus carries Europa to Crete in the form of a bull and fathers Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys by her. He is also recorded as the father of Hellen by Pyrrha or as Hellen's possible father, the father of the Graces, and the husband of Themis by whom the Fates are born. He sends a storm on the Greeks and later sends Harmonia and Cadmus to the Elysian Fields.

Hera, daughter of Cronus and

Zeus puts Hera in bonds and hangs her from Olympus, while also being afraid of her. Zeus and Hera refer their dispute to Tiresias as arbiter; Zeus later makes Menelaus immortal.

Herb, magical, which brings dead

Zeus is associated with many events in the unit, including sending Hermes to Deucalion and ordering Hermes to steal Io in the form of a cow. He gives the winged horses to, and is connected with, several mythological figures; he receives sacrifices, grants Hercules immortality, and is involved in the myths of the Hesperides’ apples and the death of Iasion.

Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares

Zeus is the father of the Muses by Mnemosyne and of several other figures named in the unit. He swallows Metis after learning of a prophecy concerning her son, hangs Hera from Olympus, turns nymphs into the Hyades, and has encounters with Nemesis in different forms.

Omphale, mistress of Hercules,

Zeus was the father of Order and Peace by Themis, of Pan by Hybris, and of Persephone by Styx. He also fathered Perseus by Danae and granted the Palladium to Ilus.

Ram with golden fleece carries

Zeus receives the sacrifice of the golden-fleeced ram, is the father of Rhadamanthys by Europa, and is the father of Sarpedon by Europa or Laodamia. He fathers the Seasons by Themis and Taygete's son Lacedaemon, ordains oaths by the water of Styx, and is involved in the births of Dionysus and Persephone.

Vine discovered by Dionysus,

Zeus was the son of Cronus and Rhea, ruler of the sky, husband of Hera, and father of numerous gods and heroes. He fought the Titans, Typhon, and the giants; ordained oaths by the water of Styx; punished or transformed many figures; and caused or ended several major events, including the great flood. He fathered or encountered figures including Athena, Dionysus, Hercules, Perseus, Helen, Castor, Pollux, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, Amphion, and Zethus, and intervened repeatedly in the affairs of gods, heroes, and cities.

Jupiter in The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII

Ovid · about AD 8 · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter is a God, king of heaven, omnipotent Father, ruler of the world and Gods, and possessor of heaven, the sceptre, thunder, and lightning. Son of Saturn and brother of Neptune and Pluto, he rules after Saturn is driven into Tartarus, shortens perpetual spring, and divides the year into four periods. When Giants seek heaven, he fights them with lightning, breaks their mountain structure, and buries them beneath mountains. Confronting human corruption, he visits Lycaon, punishes him by turning him into a wolf and burning his house, then resolves on a universal deluge. He sends rain rather than thunder, but afterward spares the guiltless Deucalion and Pyrrha and clears the sky. His later actions combine judgment, power, and repeated disguises or sexual pursuits: he changes Io into a heifer, has Epaphus by her, and has Argus killed; he strikes Phaëton with lightning to restrain world-threatening flames; he deceives and assaults Calisto in Diana's form and fathers Arcas; and, as a bull, carries Europa to Crete. He is also father of Mercury, Perseus, Bacchus, Æacus, and others named in the records. He approaches Semele with moderated thunder but still burns her, grants Tiresias prophetic knowledge, and mediates between Ceres and Pluto over Proserpine, dividing the year between them. Near the end, he answers Æacus with lightning and thunder and changes ants into men to supply Æacus with a new people. The records also say several persons may have borne his name, making some adventures uncertainly assigned.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

34 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter

Jupiter slays the Giants, changes Lycaon into a wolf, and destroys the human race and animals by a Deluge. He later strikes Phaëton with a thunderbolt, assumes the form of Diana to approach Calisto, and carries Europa over the sea after assuming the form of a bull.

opening

Jupiter rules the world after Saturn is driven into Tartarus. He shortens the former perpetual spring and divides the year into winter, summer, autumn, and spring.

notes .. notes

Jupiter treated Saturn as Saturn had treated his father Uranus. Jupiter also waged war against the Giants when they attempted to dispossess him of the heavens.

opening

Jupiter, called the omnipotent Father, hurls lightning at the Giants, breaks through their mountain structure, and strikes Ossa away from Pelion.

notes .. notes

Jupiter is associated with the war against the Titans, which is presented as distinct from the war of the giants.

opening

Jupiter beholds the crimes of the human race, recalls Lycaon's polluted banquet, and summons a council of the Gods. He declares that the race of mortals must be destroyed because their corruption cannot be cured, and says that he descended from Olympus in human form to examine the earth and found the reality worse than reported.

notes .. notes

Jupiter calls the Gods to a grand council to deliberate upon the punishment of mankind for its wickedness.

opening

Jupiter visits Lycaon's palace and gives a sign that a God has come, prompting the people to worship him. In punishment for Lycaon's crimes, Jupiter destroys the house and transforms Lycaon into a wolf; he then declares that all wicked men deserve vengeance.

notes .. notes

Jupiter is the deity before whom Lycaon is said to have set human flesh. In the explanation, Jupiter is also associated with an altar at Lycosura where human victims were sacrificed.

opening

Jupiter resolves to destroy the corrupt human race by a universal deluge. He chooses rain rather than thunderbolts, sends the South Wind, releases the rains from the whole tract of Heaven, and commands that the rest of the punishment be left to his care.

opening

Jupiter sees that the world has been overwhelmed and that only Deucalion and Pyrrha remain, both guiltless and worshippers of the gods. He disperses the clouds, removes the showers with the North Wind, and exposes the Earth and the heavens to one another.

notes .. notes

Jupiter is described as one of three brothers who may originally have been kings of separate kingdoms. After being deified, he was depicted as retaining sovereignty over his kingdom in the division of the world.

opening

Jupiter sees Io returning from her father's stream and pursues her. He invites her into the groves, promises protection, covers the earth with darkness, stops her flight, and ravishes her.

notes .. notes

Jupiter carried Io away and had Epaphus by her. After Juno placed Io under Argus's care, Jupiter killed Argus and placed Io aboard a vessel with a cow's figure at its head.

opening

Jupiter changes Io into a sleek heifer to conceal her from Juno. When Juno demands the cow as a gift, Jupiter gives Io up despite his love and shame, then sends Mercury to kill Argus.

opening

Jupiter embraces Juno and entreats her to end Io’s punishment, promising that Io will never again trouble her. He swears this by calling the Stygian waters to hear the oath, and Epaphus is believed to have been born from his seed.

opening .. opening

Jupiter calls the Gods and the giver of the chariot to witness the danger, then hurls a poised lightning bolt at Phaëton. The bolt kills Phaëton, destroys his seat, and restrains the flames.

opening

Jupiter excuses the hurling of his lightnings and adds threats to the Gods’ entreaties that darkness not be brought over the world. Phaëton’s father challenges Jupiter to drive the chariot so that he may experience the strength of the flame-footed steeds.

opening

Jupiter sees Calisto while surveying the restored earth and desires her. He assumes the form and dress of Diana, deceives Calisto, and assaults her despite her resistance before returning to heaven.

notes .. notes

Jupiter is identified as Calisto’s lover and the father of Arcas. He prevents Arcas from killing the bear who is his mother and places Calisto and Arcas in the heavens.

opening

Jupiter is Mercury's father. Mercury invokes Jupiter's identity while asking Aglauros to favor him in his love for Herse.

opening

Jupiter disguises himself as a white bull after directing the herd toward the shore. He mingles with the oxen, behaves gently toward Europa, and carries her across the ocean.

notes .. notes

The text says that several persons may have borne the name Zeus or Jupiter, making it difficult to assign particular adventures to each one. It attributes various myths to different Jupiters, including the abduction of Ganymede, the deception of Leda, and the abduction of Europa.

BOOK THE THIRD.

Jupiter carries away Europa while disguised as a bull, then lays aside that shape and reveals himself in the Dictæan land. His intrigues are unknown to Cadmus, who searches for Europa without knowing what has happened to her.

opening

Jupiter promises Semele that she may choose any favor and swears that he will not deny it. After she makes her request, he regrets having sworn but prepares to approach with clouds, winds, rain, lightning, thunder, and the thunderbolt.

notes .. notes

Jupiter was one of the princes associated with the intrigue involving Semele. After Semele was taken to heaven, she ate at the same table as Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Venus.

opening

Jupiter visits Semele while using a less destructive form of thunder, but its divine force still burns her. Later, after drinking nectar, he disputes with Juno about whether females or males experience greater sexual pleasure, and he grants Tiresias knowledge of future events after Juno blinds him.

notes .. notes

Jupiter was said to be the father of several accounts of Bacchus, including the Theban Bacchus, whose mother was Semele. One explanation of Bacchus’s birth says that Jupiter carried him in his thigh, a story possibly based on a Greek word that can also mean the hollow of a mountain.

opening

Jupiter is identified as the father of Perseus and as the ancestor of Bacchus. Acrisius first denies that Perseus is Jupiter’s offspring, but later regrets not acknowledging his grandson.

notes .. notes

Jupiter was said to be the father of Perseus by Danaë, having seduced her in the form of a shower of gold. He was also identified as the father of Bacchus and an ancestor of Acrisius through Belus.

notes .. notes

Jupiter is described in one interpretation as a Titan king who received the west in the partition of the world. In the allegorical explanation, he decided the dispute between Ceres and Pluto, symbolizing the earth’s becoming covered with crops again.

opening

Jupiter receives Ceres’s appeal and says that Proserpine is a charge shared by him and Ceres. He agrees that Proserpine may return to heaven if she has touched no food in the Infernal Regions.

opening

Jupiter mediates between Pluto and Ceres and divides the rolling year equally between them.

opening

Jupiter responds to Æacus's prayer by giving a sign through lightning and propitious thunder. He transforms the ants near his sacred oak into men, providing Æacus with a new people.
