Jupiter in The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV

Ovid · about AD 8 · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter is a god, supreme ruler and king of the Gods, yet governed by the Fates like the other gods. He is a father and ancestor: parent of Mercury, Æacus, Minos, Venus, and Hercules; grandfather of Peleus through Æacus; and father of the Gods. His actions combine disguise, desire, judgment, transformation, and deification. Disguised as a man with Mercury, he visits Philemon and Baucis, rewards their hospitality, punishes their impious neighborhood, turns their cottage into a temple, and grants their request. Taking Amphitryon’s form, he deceives Alcmena, prolongs the night, and becomes Hercules’s father; later he receives Hercules’s immortal part into the celestial regions and makes him divine. He grants Calirrhoë’s sons vengeance by making them men while still children, protects travellers and wayfarers, refers the dispute over Adonis to Calliope, and becomes an eagle to carry Ganymede to Heaven as cup-bearer. He desires Thetis but yields her to Peleus because of a prophecy. He transforms Memnon’s ashes into birds, punishes the fraudulent and perjured Cercopes by changing them into hairy animals, and grants Venus’s request that Aeneas receive godhead. He also deifies Romulus by approving his translation to heaven.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

FABLE V. [VIII.547-610]

Jupiter visits the home of Philemon and Baucis disguised as a man, together with Mercury. He reveals their divine identity, punishes the impious neighborhood, transforms the cottage into a temple, and grants the couple's request.

FABLE II. [IX.101-272]

Jupiter is called Cenæan in connection with the altar Hercules prepares on Œta. He declares that Hercules's immortal part comes from him, receives it into the celestial regions, and makes Hercules a divinity.

FABLE III. [IX.273-323]

Jupiter is the father of the concealed burden Alcmena carries, namely Hercules. Alcmena angrily reproaches him during her suffering and calls him ungrateful.

EXPLANATION.

Jupiter was said to have taken the form of Amphitryon to deceive Alcmena and become the father of Hercules. Some accounts also attributed Hercules’s extraordinary strength and valour to his divine parentage and said that Jupiter prolonged the night of Hercules’s conception.

FABLE V. [IX.426-665]

Jupiter tells the other divinities that the Fates govern even the gods and that no one can overcome them. He cites Iolaüs, the sons of Calirrhoë, Rhadamanthus, Æacus, and Minos as examples of their power.

FABLE III. [X.106-142]

Jupiter became enamored of Ganymede and transformed himself into an eagle capable of carrying his bolts. In that form he carried Ganymede to Heaven and made him his cup-bearer.

FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]

Jupiter is in love with Thetis and is alarmed by the prophecy that her son will be greater than his father. He therefore avoids her embraces and has Peleus pursue her instead.

FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]

Jupiter grants Aurora's request to honor Memnon after his death. At his assent, the ashes from Memnon's funeral pyre become birds.

BOOK THE FOURTEENTH.

Jupiter, abhorring the frauds, perjuries, and crimes of the Cercopes, transforms them into ugly, hairy animals. He removes their power of speech except for a harsh jabbering.

FABLES VII. AND VIII. [XIV.441-526]

Jupiter agrees to Venus’s request that Aeneas receive godhead. He declares Venus and Aeneas worthy of the gift and grants what she asks.

Zeus in The Library

Apollodorus · about AD 70 to 200 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god, son of Cronus and Rhea, secretly born in the cave of Dicte and nursed and guarded by nymphs, Curetes, and Amalthea while Cronus is deceived with a stone. Once grown, Zeus allies with Metis, frees the Cyclopes, receives thunder, lightning, and the thunderbolt, defeats Cronus and the Titans with Cronus’s disgorged children, and gains sovereignty over the sky. He becomes a powerful ruler and punisher: he fights Giants and Typhon, uses thunderbolts against enemies and offenders, punishes Prometheus, Salmoneus, Lycaon and his sons, Capaneus, and Hera, and acts against the Curetes after Epaphus disappears. He also directs or intervenes in events involving Persephone, the Argonauts, Heracles, Tiresias, Cadmus and Harmonia, and others. His family and sexual unions are central. Zeus marries Hera and fathers Hebe, Ilithyia, and Ares; he fathers many further children by goddesses and mortal women, including the Seasons, Fates, Graces, Persephone, the Muses, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Tityus, Hellen, Aethlius, Argos, Epaphus, Perseus, Hercules, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, and others attributed to him in particular accounts. He repeatedly changes form or appearance in these affairs: into gold for Danae, Amphitryon’s likeness for Alcmena, a tame bull for Europa, and disguises associated with Artemis or Apollo for Callisto. He transforms or causes transformations, including Io into a white cow, Callisto into a bear, Ceyx and Alcyone into birds, Dionysus into a kid, and Laelaps and the vixen into stone. The record closes with Zeus testing Lycaon’s family in a day-labourer’s form, punishing their impiety, and concealing Callisto from Hera.

BOOK I

Zeus was the son of Cronus and Rhea. Rhea gave birth to him secretly in a cave of Dicte and arranged for the Curetes and the nymphs Adrastia and Ida to nurse and guard him, while Cronus swallowed a stone believing it was the newborn child.

II. ᾿Ἐ ππειδὴ δὲ Ζεὺς ἐγενήθη τέλειος, λαμβάνει

When Zeus becomes full-grown, he takes Metis as his helper and wages war against Cronus and the Titans with the aid of the children Cronus had swallowed. He frees the Cyclopes, receives thunder, lightning, and a thunderbolt from them, defeats the Titans, and is allotted sovereignty over the sky.

III. Ζεὺς δὲ γαμεῖ μὲν “Ἥραν, καὶ τεκνοῖ

Zeus married Hera and fathered Hebe, Ilithyia, and Ares with her. He fathered Aphrodite by Dione, the Graces by Eurynome, Persephone by Styx, and the Muses by Mnemosyne, and he had intercourse with many mortal and immortal women. He swallowed Metis while she was pregnant, and Athena later emerged from his head.

Zeus pursued Asteria and Leto. He was the father of Apollo, Artemis, and Tityus according to the accounts given in this unit.

Zeus helps Pluto secretly carry off Persephone. Later, Zeus orders Pluto to send Persephone back.

VI. Περὶ μὲν οὖν Δήμητρος ταῦτα λέγεται"

Zeus learns that the Giants cannot be killed by gods alone but can be destroyed with the help of a mortal. He prevents the Dawn, Moon, and Sun from shining, obtains the herb sought by Earth, and summons Heracles through Athena. During the battle he strikes Porphyrion with a thunderbolt, destroys other Giants with thunderbolts, and later defeats Typhon after recovering his severed sinews.

VII. Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς ἀνθρώ-

Zeus pursues Typhon with thunderbolts and buries him under Mount Etna. He punishes Prometheus for giving fire to human beings by ordering Hephaestus to nail him to Mount Caucasus. Zeus later sends Hermes to Deucalion and allows him to choose what he wants.

The people of Elis sacrifice to him at several altars, including the temple altar, the great altar made from sacrificial debris, and altars associated with cleansing, lightning, and other aspects of Zeus.

Zeus in Description of Greece

Pausanias · about AD 155 to 175 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a god worshipped through temples, altars, groves, sacrifices, priesthoods, festivals, statues, and votive offerings across Piraeus, Athens, Nemea, Ægina, Messenia, and Olympia. He is represented with varied titles and powers: Eleutherius, Counsellor, Guardian of the city, Milichian, Nemean, Pan-Hellenian, of Ithome, of the Market-Place, Supreme, Decider of Fate, and God of Oaths. His images bear such attributes as a sceptre, Victory, thunderbolts, eagles, javelins, lilies, and Ganymede; one Piraeus statue was gold and held a sceptre and Victory. Records connect him with Athene’s birth from his head; fatherhood of Zethus and Amphion; Ægina and Æacus; rain after drought; foreknowledge of human events; and transformations or deceptions involving a cuckoo and the appearance of Amphitryon. The account begins with his cult image at Piraeus and Athene’s birth, then moves through ancient altars, sacrifices, temples, and local traditions. It tells of Zeus producing settlers for Ægina, being reared by Ithome and Neda in Messenian tradition, and receiving extensive honor at Olympia. There, his temple, statue, altars, oath ritual, and numerous offerings culminate the record, showing him as a central recipient of public worship, civic guardianship, rain, prophecy, and formal oaths.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

12 sections; each heading opens the text

Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.

Zeus was worshipped in temples and represented in statues at Piraeus, Phalerum, and Athens. At Piraeus his statue was of gold and held a sceptre and Victory; in Athens he appeared as Zeus Eleutherius and Zeus the Counsellor.

CHAPTER XIV.

Zeus is associated with the ancient temple of Olympian Zeus, a shrine of Cronos and Rhea, and a grove dedicated to Earth under the title of Olympian. A statue of Zeus is also said to have given a sign of future prosperity to Seleucus when sacrificial wood moved toward it and ignited.

CHAPTER XXIV.

Zeus is represented as the recipient of Earth’s supplication for rain and as the Guardian of the city in a statue by Leochares. At the altar of Zeus the Guardian of the city, barley is placed unwatched so that a sacrificial ox eats it, after which an ox-killer throws an axe at the ox and flees; the axe is then brought to court as the defendant.

CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who

Milichian Zeus has an ancient altar on the far side of the Cephisus. Theseus was purified there after slaying the progeny of Phytalus.

CHAPTER VI.

Zeus was named as the father of Antiope's sons in the verses of Asius. The text also quotes Hesiod concerning Zeus bringing down the pride of many cities.

CHAPTER XII.

Zeus is honored at Nemea, where the Argives sacrifice to Nemean Zeus and select his priest. Zeus also appears in traditions at the temple of Hera, including the story that he changed himself into a cuckoo while courting Hera.

CHAPTER XXIX.

Zeus took Ægina, the daughter of Asopus, to the island that received her name, and he produced settlers from the soil when Æacus asked for inhabitants. Through the intervention of Æacus, Zeus was propitiated as Pan-Hellenian Zeus and brought rain to Greece after a drought.

CHAPTER XXIX.

The Messenians said that Zeus was reared among them, with Ithome and Neda as his nurses. They worshipped Zeus of Ithome at a temple supplied with water from Clepsydra, kept his statue by an annually chosen priest, and celebrated an annual feast that originally included a musical contest.

CHAPTER VIII.

The temple at Olympia was dedicated to Zeus and contained his statue. Its decoration included a golden Victory in the middle of the gable, a golden shield bearing the Gorgon Medusa, and other votive offerings.

CHAPTER XV.

Zeus is honored at Olympia by altars including those of Zeus of the Market-Place, Zeus Supreme, and the Decider of Fate. The Decider of Fate is explained as a title of Zeus because he fore-knows human events, including what the Fates send.

CHAPTER XVIII.

Zeus is represented among the statues and votive offerings at Olympia, and fines imposed on dishonest athletes were used to make statues of him. The chest also contains mythological scenes connected with Zeus, including his deception of Alcmena by assuming the appearance of Amphitryon.

CHAPTER XXII.

Zeus is represented by many statues and votive offerings at Olympia, made by cities and private individuals. His statues hold or are accompanied by attributes including thunderbolts, eagles, javelins, sceptres, lilies, and Ganymede, while the statue of Zeus the God of Oaths is used for formal oaths.

Zeus in Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II

Pausanias · about AD 155 to 175 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a deity worshiped under several names and represented by statues, altars, precincts, temples, and an oracle. At Dodona, he warns the Athenians about the Areopagus and the smoking altars of the Eumenides and orders protection for defeated Lacedæmonians as suppliants. As Zeus Lycæus, he is linked to Lycaon, the Lycæa, Mount Lycæus, secret sacrifices, and rites during drought; Arcadians and Methydrium people place his birth or rearing there. He has precincts and a stone temple at Megalopolis, while Zeus Eleutherius has an altar and white-stone statue at Platæa. His actions include an intrigue with Callisto, ordering Hermes to save her child and making that child the Great Bear; sending the Fates to grieving Demeter; and using a dressed wooden statue and a proposed marriage to Platæa to reconcile Hera. He is also called Lecheates, is father of Dionysus through Semele, and receives a sceptre from Hephæstus.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

9 sections; each heading opens the text

CHAPTER XXV.

Zeus at Dodona warned the Athenians to remember the Areopagus and the smoking altars of the Eumenides. He instructed them to treat the Lacedæmonians conquered in battle as inviolable suppliants.

CHAPTER II.

Zeus Lycæus was the deity whom Lycaon called by that name and to whom he established the Lycæa. Lycaon sacrificed a baby on his altar.

CHAPTER III.

Zeus had an intrigue with Callisto. He sent Hermes to save the child with which Callisto was pregnant and turned the child into the constellation known as the Great Bear.

CHAPTER XXX.

Lycæan Zeus has precincts and a stone temple in the market-place of Megalopolis. The temple has no approach, but its interior is visible; it contains altars, two tables, and two eagles.

CHAPTER XXXVI.

The people of Methydrium say that Rhea bore Zeus on part of Mount Lycæeus and sought protection for him at Mount Thaumasium. They also locate there the deception of Cronos, in which a stone was offered instead of the child.

CHAPTER XXXVIII.

The Arcadians say Zeus was reared on Mount Lycæus, at a place called Cretea, by the Nymphs Thisoa, Neda, and Hagno. Lycæan Zeus receives secret sacrifices at an altar on the mountain, and a priest prays to him and performs a customary sacrifice when drought harms the land.

CHAPTER XLII.

Zeus learned from Pan where Demeter was hidden and sent the Fates to persuade her to abandon her anger and grief.

CHAPTER II.

Zeus Eleutherius is honored at Platæa by an altar and a statue, both described as being near the tombs of those who fell against the Medes. The statue is made of white stone.

CHAPTER III.

When Hera could not be appeased, Zeus sought Cithæron's advice. He dressed a wooden statue as a bride and announced that he intended to marry Platæa, thereby prompting Hera's return and reconciliation.

Zeus in The Fall of Troy

Quintus Smyrnaeus · about AD 200 to 299 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is a supreme, immortal god: ruler and lord of gods and men, King of Heaven, Thunderer, and Cronos' Son. He rules the Blest Gods, restrains divine conflict, commands the Fates in one combat, sanctions fate and destiny, yet is himself subject to Fate, whose outcomes do not heed any immortal. He is father of Ares, Athena, Dardanus, and Helen, and is connected with Leto. His authority appears in thunder, lightning, cloud, rain, and fire from heaven; he once destroyed the Titans with fire, and all are said to obey him because he is mightier than gods and men. During the war around Troy, Zeus's loyalties and actions vary. Though Hera reproaches him for aiding and protecting Troy, he foresees its destruction by the Argives and later ruin for the victors through war and sea. He loves both Achilles and Memnon, strengthens them for their contest, commands the Fates to stand beside them, and uses thunder to send Eos back to her course. He gives the Argives courage to behold the goddesses and rains ambrosia on Achilles' body, but also hides Troy in cloud, frightens the Argives with thunder and lightning, grants that many Trojans will perish, and kindles Neoptolemus' zeal for war. Zeus stops Ares from entering battle with thunder and lightning, and later ends fighting among the gods by threatening destruction. He clears dust and winds when armies cannot recognize one another, confirms Calchas's counsel through thunder, and does not grant all Argives safe return. Finally, he gives Athena weapons wrought by the Cyclopes, supports her storm with thunder and rain, and helps enable Poseidon and Apollo to destroy the Achaean walls at Troy.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

But on the grave-mound of Menoetius' son

Zeus sends thunder and lightning before Ares to stop him from entering the battle. Ares recognizes Zeus's threat and submits to his authority.

Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son

Zeus loves both Achilles and Memnon and gives each extraordinary strength during their contest. He commands the Fates to stand beside them, and his thunder causes Eos to return to her course.

So the kings drew him from that stricken field

Zeus fills the Argive men with courage so they can behold the gathered goddesses, and he rains ambrosia on Achilles' body during the funeral preparations. At Thetis' lament, Calliope warns her not to provoke Zeus, and Poseidon later says that Achilles will rise to the light of Zeus.

BOOK IV

Zeus is reproached by Hera for helping Troy despite his connection to Peleus and Thetis’ marriage. He remains silent while thinking that the Argives will soon destroy Priam’s city and that he will later bring ruin upon the victors by war and sea.

Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached

Zeus responds to Ganymedes by covering Troy and its walls with a vast pall of cloud, drowning the battle in mist, and sending thunder and lightning that frighten the Argives. Neleus' son recalls that Zeus once destroyed the presumptuous Titans with fire and says that all must obey him because he is mightier than gods and men.

BOOK IX

Zeus hears Antenor's prayer and grants that many of Troy's people will perish, but he does not turn Neoptolemus away from the city. Instead, he further kindles Neoptolemus' zeal for war so that Thetis may receive grace and glory.

BOOK XI

Zeus, called Cronion, clears away the dust and calms the deadly winds when the armies can no longer distinguish friend from foe. The text says that Fate does not heed Zeus or any other immortal in determining its outcomes.

BOOK XII

Zeus's thunder and lightning confirm Calchas's counsel and frighten Neoptolemus and Philoctetes into obeying the plan. Later, Zeus interrupts the fighting among the gods by threatening their destruction, causing them to end their conflict.

BOOK XIV.

Zeus is called the sire of Helen and is said to sanction the deeds of Destiny. The Argives pray to him for a safe return, but he does not grant return to all of them.

When nigh Euboea's windy heights they drew,

Zeus hears Athena's complaint and grants her the weapons made for him by the Cyclopes. He watches with joy as she brings the storm, thunders in support of her purpose, and pours rain that helps Poseidon and Apollo destroy the Achaean walls at Troy.

Jupiter in Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable

Thomas Bulfinch · 1855 · the work’s page · read it where Jupiter first appears

Abstract written by a model

Jupiter is a god: the son of Kronos, also called Saturn, and Rhea, also called Ops; a king of gods and men; and the real monarch of heaven. After defeating Saturn and the Titans, he rules the heavens with thunderbolts, the Aegis, and the eagle as his favored bird. His power governs both gods and mortals: he summons councils, directs Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo, hears prayers, gives judgments, and has oracles at Dodona and the Libyan oasis of Jupiter Ammon. He can punish on a vast scale, sending Pandora after the theft and acceptance of fire, resolving to destroy corrupt mankind by flood, and destroying an inhospitable village while sparing Baucis and Philemon. Yet he also spares Deucalion and Pyrrha, answers Aeacus by creating a new population for Aegina, grants Psyche immortality, and gives Endymion perpetual youth joined to sleep. His thunder punishes figures including Salmoneus and Aesculapius. His life is also marked by marriage, desire, disguises, and fatherhood. Though husband of Juno and unfaithful to her, he pursues Io, protects her through Mercury’s killing of Argus, and ultimately secures her restoration. He carries Europa away as a bull, enters Danae’s apartment as a shower of gold, and is father of Perseus, Minerva, Bacchus, Hercules, and others. He seeks Thetis but withdraws after learning her son would surpass his father. In later actions, he supports the Trojans at Thetis’s request, restrains Neptune, aids Hector through Apollo, permits and protects Sarpedon’s death, and clears darkness after Ajax’s prayer. Across these records, Jupiter remains the supreme ruler whose decisions bring destruction, protection, transformation, and divine order.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

15 sections; each heading opens the text

Chapter I

Jupiter, or Zeus, was the real monarch of heaven and the father of gods and men. He was the son of Saturn and Ops, defeated Saturn and the Titans, ruled the heavens, wielded the thunder, and carried the shield called the Aegis; the eagle was his favorite bird.

CHAPTER II

Jupiter sent Pandora to punish Prometheus, Epimetheus, and man for the theft and acceptance of fire. Angered by human corruption, he decided to destroy mankind, changed his plan from burning the world to drowning it, and summoned Neptune's aid. He later spared Deucalion and Pyrrha after seeing their harmless and pious lives.

Chapter III

Jupiter changes Io into a heifer when Juno approaches, gives her to Juno when refusing would arouse suspicion, and later sends Mercury to kill Argus. He intercedes for Io and promises Juno that he will not pay her any more attentions, leading Juno to restore Io's human form. Jupiter also rescues Callisto and her son from death and places them in the heavens as the Great and Little Bear.

Chapter IV

Jupiter visited Phrygia in human shape with his son Mercury and was refused shelter by many inhabitants. He revealed himself as a god, spared Baucis and Philemon, destroyed the inhospitable village by flooding it, and transformed their cottage into a temple.

CUPID AND PSYCHE

Jupiter listens favorably when Cupid pleads for Psyche and Cupid's marriage. He persuades Venus to consent and gives Psyche ambrosia, making her immortal.

Chapter VII

Jupiter carries Europa away to Crete while disguised as a bull. He is worshiped by Cadmus and Aeacus, and he responds to Aeacus's prayer by providing a new population for Aegina through the transformation of ants.

PERSEUS AND MEDUSA

Jupiter sees and loves Danae, entering her apartment as a shower of gold. He is the father of Perseus.

Chapter X

Jupiter took the form of a ram when the giants frightened the gods into fleeing to Egypt, and he was later worshipped there as Ammon. He also sent a gadfly that caused Pegasus to throw Bellerophon, and he struck Aesculapius with lightning at Pluto's request.

Chapter XII

Jupiter was the father of Hercules and declared that the hero's divine nature could not be destroyed by the flames on Mount Oeta. He took Hercules to heaven in a four-horse chariot and later gave him Hebe in marriage.

Chapter XIV

Jupiter is Semele’s lover and the father of Bacchus. He swears an irrevocable oath by the Styx to grant Semele a request, then appears to her in divine splendor; her mortal body cannot endure the radiance, and she is consumed.

Chapter XV

Jupiter seeks Thetis in marriage but abandons the attempt after learning from Prometheus that her son will be greater than his father. He then decrees that she will marry a mortal.

Chapter XVI

Jupiter sent a thunderbolt against Aesculapius after Pluto became alarmed that the healer restored the dead to life. He later punished Apollo by requiring him to serve a mortal for one year, and in another account gave a magical horn to the nurses of his infancy.

Chapter XIX

Jupiter was said to have granted Endymion perpetual youth joined with perpetual sleep. He also changed the sparks and cinders of Memnon’s funeral-pyre into birds that fought over the pyre each year.

THE ILIAD

Jupiter agrees to Thetis's request that the Trojans succeed so the Greeks will regret their treatment of Achilles. He later orders Neptune away and Apollo to aid Hector, permits Sarpedon's death, protects Sarpedon's remains, and clears the darkness after Ajax's prayer.

MYTH OF OSIRIS AND ISIS

Jupiter had an oracle at Dodona and another at the Libyan oasis of Jupiter Ammon. At Dodona, responses were believed to come through the sounds of oak branches interpreted by priests.

is_a chief deity of Thebes [king of the gods; the concealed sun] Amen Ra was a human-form deity crowned with a flat-topped cap and two long plumes, and he was generally described as King of the Gods and chief deity of Thebes. Chapter XXVII

Amen Ra was a human-form deity crowned with a flat-topped cap and two long plumes, and he was generally described as King of the Gods and chief deity of Thebes. He was also identified as the concealed sun, and his name appeared in Greek and Latin writers as Zeus Ammon and Jupiter Ammon.

Zeus in Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone

Sophocles · 1912 · the work’s page · read it where Zeus first appears

Abstract written by a model

Zeus is an all-seeing god and lord of heaven, invoked as witness and protector. His power aids the guardian host, and he strikes the boastful, impious invading Argive host with lightning.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

2 sections; each heading opens the text

CHORUS.

Zeus is called all-seeing and lord of heaven. The Chorus asks him to give the guardian host strength to surprise the fleeing foes and win their prize.

ANTIGONE

Zeus is invoked as a witness to Creon’s policy of putting the state first. The Chorus says that Zeus struck the invading Argive host with lightning because of its boastfulness and impiety.
